summary: This informational RFC presents an approach to offering Layer 2 VPN services, including Ethernet VPNs, using BGP for auto-discovery and signaling. It aims to give customers an experience like traditional L2VPNs while letting providers run it on their IP and MPLS infrastructure rather than a separate network for each service.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 6624 shows how a network provider can offer private Layer 2 connections, the kind that carry a customer's own Ethernet or Frame Relay traffic, over the same IP and MPLS network it already uses for everything else. The provider's edge routers use BGP, the protocol routers use to exchange routes, to find each other's customers automatically, so most of the hand configuration goes away.

subtitle: Private Layer 2 circuits carried over one shared IP and MPLS network, with BGP used to find the customer sites.

tldr.problem: Providers that sold Layer 2 private circuits ran a separate network for each kind of connection, and had to configure every switch by hand for every customer circuit.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC applies the auto-discovery and signalling already used for Layer 3 VPNs to Layer 2 VPNs. BGP advertises which customer sites exist, Route Targets decide which sites see each other, and an MPLS label tells the tunnel which circuit a frame belongs to.
tldr.outcome: A provider can run Layer 2 VPNs, IP VPNs and the Internet on one network, and adding a customer site becomes a local task at the new site and the edge router it plugs into.

facts.label: Full-mesh circuits
facts.value: n*(n-1)/2 DLCI PVCs across the provider network

today: RFC 6624 is an Informational RFC published in May 2012, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It describes an approach rather than a protocol standard: it names RFC 4447 and RFC 6074 as the standards that cover the same signalling functions, and recommends implementing those as well.

sections.title: Why Layer 2 VPNs Cost So Much
sections.content:
A Layer 2 VPN gives a customer private connections between its sites by carrying the customer's own link-layer traffic across the provider's network. The hand-off happens at Layer 2, so the customer keeps control of its own addressing and can run whatever network protocols it likes over the connection.

The RFC points at two separate costs. The first was infrastructure. The easiest way to offer a Layer 2 VPN of one kind was to build a network of that same kind, so an ATM network for ATM VPNs, an Ethernet network for Ethernet VPNs, and yet another for the Internet and IP VPNs. The second cost was provisioning. Only the provisioning system knew that two separate circuits belonged to the same VPN, so each switch had to be told the address of every other switch in that VPN.

That second cost made a full mesh expensive. Each switch in the VPN had to know about every other switch, and setting up even one circuit often meant provisioning every switch along the path. The RFC's aim is to keep the customer experience of a traditional Layer 2 VPN while removing both costs.
sections.plainLanguage: A Layer 2 VPN carries a customer's own traffic between its sites. Building one used to mean running a separate network for each kind of connection and configuring every switch by hand, and a full mesh of sites made that work grow with the square of the number of sites.

sections.title: What the Provider Gets Out of It
sections.content:
The RFC lists the advantages of keeping the provider out of customer routing. The provider is responsible for Layer 2 connectivity and the customer for Layer 3 routing, so a customer router that misbehaves can flap its own interface without disturbing the provider's network, whereas in a Layer 3 VPN a customer edge router can destabilise the provider's edge router or even the whole network.

Because the provider never handles customer routes, there are no per-VPN routing tables at the edge and the privacy of routing comes for free. The customer can also run any Layer 3 protocol it likes, rather than having to match whatever the provider runs. Moving from a real Frame Relay circuit to a tunnelled one changes almost nothing for the customer, because the two are indistinguishable from the customer's point of view.

Scaling also favours Layer 2. Each provider edge router keeps a single small record per customer site and a single route per site, so its tables scale with the number of sites rather than with the number of routes the customer sends. A Layer 3 VPN has the opposite property, since a customer edge router may advertise an arbitrary number of routes, which is why a provider has to cap how many routes it will accept from one customer.
sections.plainLanguage: Keeping the provider out of customer routing keeps customer problems away from the provider's network, hides customer routes from everyone else, and lets the customer use any network protocol it wants. The provider's tables stay small because they hold one entry per site.

sections.title: The Parts of a Layer 2 VPN
sections.content:
The roles are standard. The device in the customer site is the CE (customer edge); the provider router it connects to is the PE (provider edge); a provider router that touches no customer is a P router. Each pair of PE routers is joined by a tunnel, and inside the tunnel the individual circuits are told apart by a demultiplexor, which in this document is an MPLS label.

Each CE connection within a VPN is given a CE ID, a number that identifies it uniquely inside that VPN. A CE with several connections has one CE ID for each. A physical connection from a CE to a PE can carry several attachment circuits, and the logical connection that joins two attachment circuits across the provider network is a pseudowire.

Provisioning is where the savings come from. In a full-mesh Frame Relay VPN with n sites, n*(n-1)/2 DLCI permanent virtual circuits must be provisioned across the provider network, each CE needs n-1 DLCIs, and each circuit needs state in every transit switch. The RFC's answer is overprovisioning: give each CE more circuits than it needs today, and map a CE ID to a circuit by a simple local rule. Adding a site then needs only the new CE and its PE to be configured, after which the PE advertises a BGP Layer 2 route and the other PEs set up the path.
sections.plainLanguage: The customer device is called the CE and the provider router it plugs into is the PE. Provider routers are joined by tunnels, and an MPLS label inside the tunnel says which customer circuit a frame belongs to. Overprovisioning circuits at each site means a new site needs only local configuration.

sections.title: How the Edge Routers Learn About Each Other
sections.content:
When a PE is configured for a customer site, it advertises that fact to the other PEs with BGP. BGP was chosen because it already offers mechanisms for both auto-discovery and signalling, because it lets a provider converge on one way of running all its VPN services, and because it gives a robust answer for VPNs that cross more than one operator's network.

Two changes to the BGP messages are needed. The set of encapsulation types carried in the L2-info extended community is widened, and the value in that field names the Layer 2 technology in use, from Frame Relay to Ethernet to PPP. Second, TLVs (type-length-value triplets) are added to the VPLS network layer reachability information. In these TLVs the Type field is one octet and the Length field is two octets, and it gives the size of the Value field in bits. L2VPN TLVs appear as the last element of the reachability information.

The first TLV defined is the circuit status vector, with TLV Type 1. Its Value field is a bit vector with one bit per label in the label block: a bit of 0 means the local circuit and the tunnel path to the remote PE are up, and a bit of 1 means one or both are down. The value is padded to the nearest octet boundary. A PE holding a label block from a remote PE reads the bit at the index of the remote CE to learn whether the circuit to that CE is up.
sections.plainLanguage: Provider edge routers tell each other about customers over BGP, the same protocol they use for internet routing. The RFC widens the list of connection types BGP can carry and adds a way to report whether each customer circuit is working.

sections.title: Mixing Different Layer 2 Technologies
sections.content:
By default every site in a Layer 2 VPN must reach the provider with the same Layer 2 encapsulation, so a Frame Relay site and an Ethernet site cannot share a VPN. The RFC's answer is to base interworking on IP: assume the network layer is IP, and let the provider carry only the IP packet between sites that use different encapsulation types. The trade-off is that the customer then loses the freedom to run non-IP protocols.

In this mode the ingress PE notes the Layer 2 address, strips the whole Layer 2 header, adds a VPN label, puts the packet in the tunnel and forwards it. The forwarding decision is still made on the Layer 2 address the customer supplied. At the egress PE the VPN label says which CE to send to and over which virtual circuit, and the egress PE can also work out which Layer 2 encapsulation to put back on the packet. The result is a packet made of a PSN transport header, the VPN label and the IP packet, with the VPN label acting as the demultiplexing field.

All access circuits connecting CEs to PEs in a Layer 2 VPN must be configured with the same Layer 2 MTU. The MTU on the access link must be chosen so that the Layer 2 frames plus the L2VPN header do not exceed the MTU of the provider network, and Layer 2 frames that exceed it after encapsulation must be dropped.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally every site in one of these private networks must use the same kind of connection. This RFC allows different kinds on different sites as long as only IP traffic is carried, by stripping the site connection's header and adding a label that tells the far end where to deliver the packet.

sections.title: Security and Protocol Registries
sections.content:
The security discussion leans on the document this one is built on, RFC 4761. The focus is the privacy of customer data rather than its confidentiality, integrity or authentication, and the techniques RFC 4761 uses for the control plane and the forwarding path apply equally here. One difference is that the denial-of-service concerns tied to VPLS do not apply: a PE implementing this document's procedures has neither to learn MAC addresses nor to replicate packets.

The RFC asks IANA for two registries. The first is for the one-octet encapsulation type field and is named "BGP Layer 2 Encapsulation Types". The second is for the one-octet Type field of the TLVs and is named "BGP L2 TLV Types". For both, entries up to and including 127 are reviewed by experts, entries from 128 through 251 are allocated first come first served, and the values from 252 through 255 are for experimental use.

The RFC also notes that the IETF has already standardised the functions it describes, in two documents rather than one: RFC 4447 for setting up pseudowires with the Label Distribution Protocol, and RFC 6074 for setting them up with BGP. It recommends that a device implementing this approach implement those standards as well, so that the result complies with the IETF standards.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC says the security advice of the document it builds on applies here, and adds that the denial-of-service worries about Ethernet VPNs do not, because these provider routers neither learn MAC addresses nor copy packets. It also asks for two number registries so that the connection types and the extra fields have stable codes.
